frames.title: Day 7 Agenda
frames.text:
Welcome to Day 7: Finance, Invoicing, Billing and QuickBooks.

We'll start with finance foundations, then move to reconciliation and trust accounts, and spend a good block on invoice management. After that comes time tracking and QuickBooks, then expenses, payments and payroll, and we'll finish with tax, records and fraud.

By the end of today, you'll be able to support the firm's financial operations accurately: reconcile accounts, manage invoices from pre-bill to payment, track billable and non-billable time, work confidently in QuickBooks, manage the firm's cards and stay audit-ready.

frames.title: Finance Foundations
frames.text: Section 1 of 6: Finance Foundations. We'll look at your role in the firm's finances, what a real SOP needs, and the financial calendar.

frames.title: The EA/PA's Role in Finance
frames.text:
When you handle an invoice or an expense, you're a real link in the firm's money chain, not just filing paperwork.

A mistake, like two digits swapped, doesn't stay on your desk. It flows into the books, the client's bill and the firm's reports.

First, check the numbers before you pass anything on. Then, track financial tasks with dates, like any other recurring work.

frames.title: The EA/PA's Role in Finance
frames.text:
Finally, if something looks off, flag it. Don't assume someone later will catch it.

Picture this. A court-reporter invoice for the Meridian deposition arrives with the right amount but the wrong matter number. If you pass it on as is, where does that error show up next, and who has to fix it?

frames.title: What an SOP Actually Needs
frames.text: A good procedure answers five questions: why, who, how, how do we check, and who do we call when it goes wrong. Each answer is one part of a real procedure, and they come in order.

frames.title: What an SOP Actually Needs
frames.text:
First, purpose. Next, scope: exactly who it applies to. Then, procedure: the actual steps. After that, controls: the checks built in to prove it was done right. Finally, escalation: when and how to report a problem.

Now picture this. A temp starts Monday and will process vendor invoices while you're at a conference. Your written procedure says 'approve and pay as usual.' Could they follow it on day one? What would you add?

frames.title: Quick Check
frames.text:
Quick check. Which SOP element answers 'who does this process apply to?' Is it scope, escalation, controls or purpose? Take a second.

The answer is scope. Scope defines who the procedure covers; purpose explains why it exists.

frames.title: The Financial Calendar
frames.text:
Money deadlines are relentless, so keep them all on one calendar, with reminders well ahead.

Billing cycles, tax deadlines and month-end closes keep coming round. If they live in three different places, or in your memory, one of them will eventually slip.

First, set automatic reminders about a week to ten days before each deadline. Then, look at the calendar every week for what's coming up.

frames.title: The Financial Calendar
frames.text:
After that, if one type of deadline keeps slipping, give it extra buffer. Finally, check each cycle whether a date or requirement has changed.

Here's one to think through. It's mid-December. Month-end close, the trust reconciliation, the January estimated tax payment and the year-end contractor forms all fall within six weeks. Which one do you start first, and why?

frames.title: Financial KPIs for EAs/PAs
frames.text:
Three numbers tell you whether the financial side is healthy.

Start with speed. Every day an invoice sits unsent is money the firm has already earned and isn't collecting. And clients question old charges more than fresh ones.

First, track how long invoices take to go out, against a 24 to 72 hour target. Next, track reconciliation accuracy, aiming for 98 to 100 percent. Then, set an alert when a client's retainer drops below a quarter.

frames.title: Financial KPIs for EAs/PAs
frames.text:
After that, review these numbers on a set schedule. Finally, if one keeps missing, look at the process, not just effort.

Take a second with this one. The Harlow retainer dropped below 25 percent two weeks ago, but the alert went to an inbox nobody checks. The client now owes more than the retainer holds. What went wrong in the process, not just the person?

frames.title: Quick Check
frames.text:
Quick check. What's the target range for invoice turnaround time? Is it no target, whenever it gets done… one to two weeks… one to two hours… or 24 to 72 hours? Take a second.

It's 24 to 72 hours, from service completion to invoice sent. That's the benchmark target.

frames.title: Bookkeeping Basics & Compliance
frames.text:
The golden rule of bookkeeping: never approve your own transaction.

First, label each transaction as income, expense or receivable when you record it. Next, keep a clear trail: who entered it, when and from what document. Then, separate duties, even when it would save time. That separation is what makes the books trustworthy.

frames.title: Bookkeeping Basics & Compliance
frames.text:
After that, reconcile regularly, while mistakes are still easy to trace. Finally, flag anything that looks like a compliance gap straight away.

Think about this one. The usual approver is out, and you're asked to both enter and approve a $2,400 vendor payment. What do you do, and what do you suggest for next time?

frames.title: Reading Basic Financial Statements
frames.text:
You don't need to be an accountant, but you do need to read the three reports that tell a business's money story.

The profit and loss, or P&L, shows income minus expenses over a period, like a month. The balance sheet shows what the business owns and owes on one date: assets equal liabilities plus equity. The cash flow statement shows the cash that actually came in and went out. And client money in trust is never the firm's income.

frames.title: Reading Basic Financial Statements
frames.text: First, we compare each month's P&L with last month and the same month last year. Next, we check receivables, what clients owe, and how old it is. Then we watch recurring expenses for anything new or higher.

frames.title: Reading Basic Financial Statements
frames.text:
After that, we take questions to the accountant with the exact line and amount. Finally, we keep the monthly reports together, named the same way.

Try this one. The P&L shows a healthy profit last quarter, but Elias says there isn't enough cash for next month's payroll. How can both be true, and which report would you pull?

frames.title: Reconciliation & Trust Accounts
frames.text: Section 2 of 6: Reconciliation and Trust Accounts. We'll cover statement of account reconciliation, spotting discrepancies, and the core rules for client trust accounts.

frames.title: SOA Reconciliation
frames.text:
Reconciling an account comes down to one formula: opening balance, plus invoices, minus payments, plus or minus adjustments, equals closing balance.

A statement of account shows what a client owes over time. Reconciling it just means checking that formula works out exactly.

frames.title: SOA Reconciliation
frames.text: First, always work through it in that order. Next, if income doesn't match deposits, compare the bank statement with the income records first. Then, don't rebuild every report. Start from the numbers that don't match and work back.

frames.title: SOA Reconciliation
frames.text:
After that, make sure the closing balance matches exactly. Don't round away a small gap. Finally, write down what caused any adjustment.

Pause the video and work this one out. Opening balance $3,200, invoices $4,800, payments $6,000 and a $150 late fee. What's the closing balance? The client says they owe $1,850. Where do you look first?

frames.title: Reconciliation Discrepancy Detection
frames.text:
When a reconciliation doesn't balance, compare line by line, not just the totals.

Matching totals can hide real problems. Two mistakes can cancel each other out, or a payment can land on the wrong client's account and still leave the total looking perfect.

frames.title: Reconciliation Discrepancy Detection
frames.text: First, compare the ledger with the bank statement one line at a time. Next, check that credits went to the right client or account. Then, look for reversed entries that might be hiding an error.

frames.title: Reconciliation Discrepancy Detection
frames.text:
After that, run through the checklist: every invoice listed, every payment recorded and every difference explained. Finally, watch for anything that looks like a duplicate payment.

Now a scenario. A $3,000 payment from Meridian was recorded against a client with a similar name, who's now been sent a statement showing a credit. What do you correct, and who do you tell, in order?

frames.title: Client Trust Accounts (IOLTA) — Core Rules & Commingling Risk
frames.text:
Money in a client trust account belongs to the client until it's earned; it is never the firm's money to borrow.

Client money, like retainers and settlements, sits in a special trust account. Mixing it with the firm's own funds, even briefly or by accident, is called commingling. It's one of the most serious ethics violations a lawyer can commit, and it can end careers.

frames.title: Client Trust Accounts (IOLTA) — Core Rules & Commingling Risk
frames.text:
First, keep trust money and the firm's operating money in completely separate accounts. Next, only move money out of trust for a specific, documented reason, like an approved invoice or a signed disbursement. Finally, keep a running ledger for each client, showing exactly what's held for them.

Picture this. A client's $5,000 settlement check is deposited into trust today. Elias wants the $400 expert fee paid from it right away, because 'the money's there.' What has to happen before any money leaves trust?

frames.title: Trust Account Reconciliation Discipline
frames.text:
For a trust account, three numbers must always match exactly: the bank statement, the trust ledger and the total of every client's individual balance.

Check at least monthly, and right after anything unusual. A difference is never 'probably fine'; it gets traced to the exact transaction. And document every reconciliation, even the clean ones.

Take a second with this one. Your trust reconciliation is off by $1. It's 5:30 p.m. on the last day of the month, and everyone wants to leave. What do you do with that dollar?

frames.title: Invoice Management
frames.text: Section 3 of 6: Invoice Management. We'll cover billing and invoicing, pre-bill review, and following invoices through to payment.

frames.title: Billing & Invoicing
frames.text:
An invoice is simple math, rate times hours plus expenses minus any discount, but it has to be exactly right.

And beyond the total, every invoice needs three things: how much is due, when it's due and the payment terms. Without them, clients hesitate, and payment slows down.

frames.title: Billing & Invoicing
frames.text:
First, check the rate and hours against the engagement terms. Then, recheck the final math yourself. Finally, send it promptly. A perfect invoice sitting unsent doesn't bring in money.

Pause the video and try one: 12.5 hours at $350 an hour, $240 in filing fees and a 10 percent courtesy discount on the fees only. What's the total, and what else must the invoice say?

frames.title: Contract-Aware Billing
frames.text:
Know the contract's limits before you start billing.

Every client agreement can have its own rules: payment terms, late fees and sometimes a cap on hours. If you only discover the cap when the final bill goes out, it's too late.

First, track hours against the cap as you go. Then, flag it well before you reach it.

frames.title: Contract-Aware Billing
frames.text:
After that, apply late fees and terms consistently, as written. Finally, if the terms are unclear, confirm before you bill.

Here's one to think through. Harlow has gone six hours over its 40-hour cap, and nobody sent the 80 percent notice. The invoice is due to go out tomorrow. What do you tell Elias, and what are his options?

frames.title: Pre-Bill Review: Checking an Invoice Before It Goes Out
frames.text:
An invoice mistake the client finds costs far more trust than one we catch first.

A pre-bill is the draft invoice the attorney reviews before it goes out. It's our last chance to catch mistakes, and they're nearly always the same few. We prepare and check it; the attorney decides what's charged or written off.

frames.title: Pre-Bill Review: Checking an Invoice Before It Goes Out
frames.text:
First, we run the pre-bill at the same point every month. Next, we check the header: client, billing contact, matter, dates and any reference number. Then we check every time entry: matter, person, rate and a clear description. After that, costs: a receipt for each, no duplicates and markups only if allowed. Finally, the math, the retainer to apply and the terms, and we send the attorney our flags at the top.

Picture this. The Harlow pre-bill shows 42 hours in June. One entry is at last year's rate, two say only 'file review,' and a $620 court reporter cost appears twice. What goes in your note to Elias, and in what order?

frames.title: Invoice Management: Tracking, Follow-Up & Collections
frames.text:
Sending an invoice is only the halfway point. It's finished when it's paid, and a firm can do great work and still run short of cash if nobody follows invoices through.

We keep one invoice register with the number, client, matter, dates, amount, status and date paid. Our follow-up is polite, predictable and written down. And anything bigger than a reminder, like a payment plan, a late fee or collections, is the attorney's decision.

frames.title: Invoice Management: Tracking, Follow-Up & Collections
frames.text:
First, number invoices in one sequence and never reuse a number. A cancelled invoice is voided. Next, send each invoice to the right billing contact in the format the client asks for. Then, follow a set reminder schedule: before the due date, on it, then 7, 14 and 30 days late. After that, review the aging report every week and send Elias anything over 60 days. Finally, record payments the day they arrive, so nobody gets chased after paying.

Try this one. Meridian owes $18,400: $6,000 is 45 days overdue and $12,400 is 95 days overdue. No one has followed up. What do you send today, and what do you ask Elias?

frames.title: E-Billing Portals, LEDES & Client Billing Guidelines
frames.text:
For many corporate clients, an invoice that isn't in their portal, in their format, simply doesn't exist.

Many corporate clients and insurers want invoices uploaded to an e-billing portal, often in a standard file format called LEDES, with task and activity codes on each time entry. The portal checks each invoice against the client's billing rules. If it rejects the invoice or cuts lines, the firm doesn't get paid until it's fixed.

frames.title: E-Billing Portals, LEDES & Client Billing Guidelines
frames.text: First, for each e-billing client we record the portal, who holds the login, the format and codes, the deadline and the billing contact. Next, we keep their billing guidelines with the matter and note the rules that cause the most cuts. Then we make sure time entries have the right codes before the pre-bill.

frames.title: E-Billing Portals, LEDES & Client Billing Guidelines
frames.text:
After that, we upload and check the status: accepted, rejected or adjusted. Finally, we bring any cuts or rejections to the attorney and resubmit or appeal before the deadline.

Now a scenario. Harlow's insurer rejects the May invoice: 'Task code missing on 7 entries; 2 entries exceed the approved rate.' The resubmission window closes in 10 days. What do you do, and what do you need from Elias?

frames.title: Retainer Invoices & Applying Trust Funds
frames.text:
Retainers are where billing meets trust accounting, and mistakes here are ethics problems, not just accounting ones.

A retainer paid up front goes into the client trust account and stays the client's money until the firm has earned it and billed for it. Paying an invoice from it means moving money from trust to the firm's operating account. And an 'evergreen' retainer has to be topped back up to an agreed level.

frames.title: Retainer Invoices & Applying Trust Funds
frames.text: First, when a retainer arrives, we confirm it went into trust and record it on the client's ledger. Next, the invoice shows the total, the amount applied from the retainer and the balance left. Then we get the attorney's approval in writing before any transfer.

frames.title: Retainer Invoices & Applying Trust Funds
frames.text:
After that, we transfer exactly that amount and record it with the invoice number. Finally, when the balance drops below the agreed level, we send the approved top-up request.

Pause the video and work this one out. Meridian's evergreen retainer must stay at $10,000 or more. The balance is $11,200, and the June invoice is $6,800. What does the invoice show, what transfer happens, what's the new balance, and what goes to the client?

frames.title: Invoice & Payment Reconciliation
frames.text:
If payments aren't matched to the right invoices, clients get chased for bills they've already paid.

Real payments are messy: one wire can cover three invoices, a client can pay half, or a bank fee can make it arrive a little short. And at the end of each month, the total of all open invoices should match the receivables number in the books. If it doesn't, something was applied to the wrong place.

frames.title: Invoice & Payment Reconciliation
frames.text: First, we record each payment the day it arrives: date, amount, method, who paid and any reference. Next, we match it to invoice numbers. With no note, we match by exact amount, then ask the client. Then, part payments leave a balance open, and overpayments become a credit until the attorney decides.

frames.title: Invoice & Payment Reconciliation
frames.text:
Finally, a short payment caused by bank fees gets the fee recorded separately, if that's firm policy.

Picture this. Harlow Industries sends one wire of $7,425 with the note 'May invoices.' There are three open May invoices: $2,500, $3,000 and $2,000. What happened to the missing $75, how do you apply the wire, and what do you ask Harlow?

frames.title: Handling a Billing Dispute
frames.text:
A billing dispute is a request for an explanation, not an attack.

Most disputes come from honest confusion, not bad faith.

First, pull the actual records behind the charge before you reply. Next, acknowledge the dispute quickly, even before it's resolved. Finally, explain the answer with the supporting details, so the client can see how the charge was worked out.

Take a second with this one. You check the records and find the disputed charge was billed twice: once in May and again in June. How do you tell the client, and what else do you check before you reply?

frames.title: Time Tracking & QuickBooks
frames.text: Section 4 of 6: Time Tracking and QuickBooks. We'll cover real-time time tracking, billable versus non-billable hours, and the everyday QuickBooks workflows.

frames.title: Real-Time Time Tracking for Billable Work
frames.text:
Billable time becomes the client's invoice, so record it now, as you work or straight afterwards, not from memory later. The longer you wait, the less accurate it gets.

First, write enough detail to support the invoice line: what was done, for which matter. Finally, compare logged time with the billing calendar regularly, before invoices go out.

Here's one to think through. A client questions a 3.5-hour entry that says 'research.' The associate can't remember what the research was about. How would a better time entry have prevented this?

frames.title: Billable vs. Non-Billable Hours
frames.text:
Getting billable and non-billable right is the difference between an invoice that gets paid and one the client cuts.

Billable time is work the client can be charged for under their engagement letter: drafting, research, calls and court time on their matter. Non-billable is everything else, like internal admin, training, business development, or work the firm agreed not to charge. We record both, because non-billable time still shows where the hours go.

frames.title: Billable vs. Non-Billable Hours
frames.text: First, every entry gets a date, matter, time in tenths of an hour, a clear description and billable or not. Next, we check the engagement letter and the client's guidelines. Scheduling and copying are often non-billable. Then we write one task per entry, not one long block.

frames.title: Billable vs. Non-Billable Hours
frames.text:
After that, we prepare a pre-bill, so the attorney can decide any write-downs or write-offs. Finally, approved no-charge work can show on the invoice as 'no charge.'

Try this one. An associate's entry reads: '3.5, Harlow: call with client, research, drafted letter, scheduled meeting, copied exhibits.' Harlow's guidelines reject block billing and clerical time. How do you help fix it before the pre-bill?

frames.title: QuickBooks How-Tos — Step by Step
frames.text: Four everyday tasks cover most of what you'll ever do in QuickBooks. You don't need to master the whole program. Learn these four until you can do them without thinking.

frames.title: QuickBooks How-Tos — Step by Step
frames.text:
First, create an invoice: New, then Invoice, pick the client, add the lines with description, rate and hours, check the total and send. Next, record an expense: New, then Expense, pick who was paid and from which account, choose the category and attach the receipt. Then, reconcile an account: pick the account and statement date, tick every transaction that matches the bank and finish only when the difference is zero. Finally, run the overdue-invoices report, and look first at anything over 60 and 90 days. Those need a follow-up call.

If you have access, pause the video and try the invoice and the reconciliation yourself.

frames.title: QuickBooks: Billable Time, Expenses & Invoicing
frames.text:
QuickBooks can make sure every billable hour and cost reaches the invoice, but only if it's recorded the right way.

In QuickBooks Online, when we record time or a cost and tick 'Billable' for a customer, it waits. On their next invoice, QuickBooks shows everything that's waiting, and we choose what to add. So the invoice is only as good as the entries behind it.

frames.title: QuickBooks: Billable Time, Expenses & Invoicing
frames.text: First, we set up each client as a customer, and each matter under it as a sub-customer or project. Next, we record time with the person, matter, service item and rate, hours, a description, and Billable ticked. Then we record client costs, like filing fees, as billable expenses to the matter.

frames.title: QuickBooks: Billable Time, Expenses & Invoicing
frames.text:
After that, we add the waiting time and costs to the invoice, checking dates, descriptions and rates. Finally, we run the unbilled time and expenses report to catch anything left behind.

Now a scenario. At month-end, that report shows 6.2 hours for Harlow with no matter selected, and a $435 court reporter bill for Meridian that wasn't marked billable. What do you fix, and in what order, before invoices go out?

frames.title: QuickBooks Common Mistakes & Tips
frames.text:
The most common QuickBooks mistake is putting an expense in the wrong category, so when you're unsure, ask.

A classic example: recording a cost the client should reimburse as a general office expense. That one mistake breaks both the client's invoice and the firm's own books.

frames.title: QuickBooks Common Mistakes & Tips
frames.text: First, confirm the right category before you save an expense. Next, if a reconciliation isn't exactly zero, look for a missing or duplicated transaction. Don't adjust something unrelated to force it. Then, check every invoice against the engagement terms. The software will happily bill the wrong rate.

frames.title: QuickBooks Common Mistakes & Tips
frames.text:
After that, remember that the online version saves automatically. A mistake needs a proper correction, not an undo. Finally, review recent entries now and then for repeated category mistakes.

Take a second with this one. Your bank reconciliation is off by exactly $450, and you notice a $450 deposit entered twice. Where will you look first next time something is off by a round amount?

frames.title: QuickBooks: Bank Feeds, Rules & Month-End Close
frames.text:
Bank feeds save hours, but only if someone reviews them properly. Otherwise they fill the books with duplicates and guesses.

Bank feeds pull transactions from the firm's bank and card accounts into QuickBooks automatically, but each one still needs a decision. If it's already in the books, like a bill we've already paid, we match it. If it's new, we add it with a category and payee, and a customer if it's billable. Then month-end close is what makes the numbers reliable.

frames.title: QuickBooks: Bank Feeds, Rules & Month-End Close
frames.text: First, review the feed at least weekly. Next, make rules for regular items like rent or subscriptions, and check what they did. Then, exclude only true duplicates, with a note.

frames.title: QuickBooks: Bank Feeds, Rules & Month-End Close
frames.text:
After that, at month-end, clear the feed, reconcile every account, clear uncategorized items and run the reports. Finally, once the accountant confirms, set the closing date with a password.

Picture this. The feed shows a $1,200 payment to the firm's credit card company, and QuickBooks suggests 'Office expenses.' What is it really, how should it be recorded and what goes wrong if you accept the suggestion?

frames.title: Expenses, Payments & Payroll
frames.text: Section 5 of 6: Expenses, Payments and Payroll. We'll cover the firm's credit cards, expense report auditing, and payroll basics.

frames.title: Credit Cards & Card Applications
frames.text:
Review a credit card statement before you pay it, not after.

Three related jobs here. Paying the cards, where missed payments cost money and damage credit. Applying for cards, where we follow the issuer's process precisely. And tax season, which is really about keeping receipts organized all year long, not hunting for them in April.

frames.title: Credit Cards & Card Applications
frames.text: First, put card due dates on a real calendar. Next, check the statement for anything that shouldn't be there. Then, for an application, gather exactly the documents requested, no more and no less.

frames.title: Credit Cards & Card Applications
frames.text:
Finally, test yourself: could you hand over every receipt from the last 90 days quickly?

Here's one to think through. Reviewing Elias's card statement, you spot a $129 charge from an unfamiliar merchant and a hotel charged twice for the same night. What do you do before paying the bill?

frames.title: Credit Card Help: Disputes, Fraud & Lost Cards
frames.text:
When a card problem hits, the assistant is usually the first to know, and how fast you act decides how much it costs.

A billing error, or a charge we don't recognize, can be disputed with the issuer. For US credit cards, billing-error disputes should go in writing within 60 days of the statement that first showed the charge. A lost or stolen card, or suspected fraud, gets reported straight away. The issuer usually blocks it and sends a new card.

frames.title: Credit Card Help: Disputes, Fraud & Lost Cards
frames.text: First, with an unknown charge, we check receipts, the merchant's full name and whether someone else used the card. Next, for a wrong charge, we go to the merchant first, then dispute with the issuer if it isn't fixed. Then, for fraud or a lost card, we report it using the number on the card or the app, never a number from a message.

frames.title: Credit Card Help: Disputes, Fraud & Lost Cards
frames.text:
After that, when the new card arrives, we update every subscription and automatic payment. Finally, we log it all and check the next statement for the credit.

Try this one. Elias texts from an airport: his firm card was declined and he's had a fraud alert. He needs a hotel tonight, and the same card pays for three software subscriptions. What do you do, in order?

frames.title: Reconciling a Credit Card Statement
frames.text:
A card statement nobody reconciles hides lost client costs, personal charges and fraud.

Charges for a client matter, like deposition travel or a filing fee, are coded to the matter and marked billable so the firm gets the money back. Personal charges, even accidental ones, get flagged and repaid, never hidden in a business category.

frames.title: Reconciling a Credit Card Statement
frames.text: First, we download the statement and gather that month's receipts. Next, line by line, we match each charge to its receipt, confirm the purpose and assign the category and matter. Then we chase any missing receipts that week, or use the firm's missing-receipt form.

frames.title: Reconciling a Credit Card Statement
frames.text:
After that, we flag duplicates, unknown charges and personal charges to the right person. Finally, we reconcile the card in QuickBooks to the statement's ending balance and file everything together.

Now a scenario. Elias's statement has 34 charges, and you have 29 receipts. Two charges are for the Chicago deposition, one looks personal, a $64 pharmacy charge, and two have no receipt at all. How do you finish the reconciliation, and who do you contact?

frames.title: Expense Report Auditing & Approval Workflows
frames.text:
Without a receipt, there's no independent proof an expense actually happened.

Checking expense reports isn't about catching fraud after the fact. It's about making sure each expense is real before it's paid.

First, check each line against its receipt: amount, date and business purpose. Next, hold anything missing a receipt or reason until it's explained. Finally, send every report through the proper approver. Never approve your own.

Picture this. One staff member bought three laptop accessories from the same shop on the same day, at $180, $190 and $175. The limit without extra approval is $200. What do you do?

frames.title: Vendor Payment Terms & Cash Flow Timing
frames.text:
Pay vendors according to the terms you agreed, not on reflex.

Terms like 'net 30' or 'due on receipt' shape the firm's cash flow. Paying earlier than needed ties up money with no benefit, unless there's an early-payment discount. Paying late brings fees, strained relationships and sometimes cut-off service.

First, confirm each vendor's actual terms. Don't assume a default. Then, line up upcoming payments against expected money coming in, so they don't collide.

Take a second with this one. Three large vendor bills are due on the 1st, and the firm's biggest client payment is expected on the 15th. The office manager wants to pay all three immediately. What do you flag to Elias?

frames.title: Payroll Basics for EA/PA Support Roles
frames.text:
Payroll deadlines never move, so your part of it can't be late.

You probably won't run payroll yourself, but you'll touch its edges: onboarding paperwork, timesheets and reimbursements. And salaries and bank details are among the most sensitive data you'll handle.

First, make sure timesheets and hours are accurate and in before the payroll cut-off. Next, handle new-hire forms and bank changes as confidential documents. Finally, put payroll deadlines on the compliance calendar with the other hard deadlines.

Here's one to think through. A colleague asks you what the new associate earns, 'just roughly.' You processed the offer letter. How do you answer?

frames.title: Tax, Records & Fraud
frames.text: Section 6 of 6: Tax, Records and Fraud. We'll cover tax season support, record retention and fraud red flags in financial documents.

frames.title: Tax Season Support & Working with Accountants
frames.text:
Tax season is easy when you've filed everything properly all year long.

The real value you bring at tax time isn't a heroic effort in March. It's the habit of organizing receipts, invoices and records every week, so when the accountant asks for something, you simply find it instead of rebuilding a year from memory.

First, become the person who can reliably answer 'do you have this?'

frames.title: Tax Season Support & Working with Accountants
frames.text:
After that, connect it to reconciliation: good records make reconciling fast. Finally, build a small daily or weekly filing habit instead of one giant push a year.

Try this one. The accountant asks for all of last year's business travel receipts by Wednesday. Half are filed by date and trip; half are photos in Elias's phone. What do you do now, and what habit do you start for this year?

frames.title: Quarterly Tax Schedules
frames.text:
Quarterly estimated taxes are four separate deadlines, each with its own lead time.

Missing one brings penalties. It's the same reminder discipline we use for court deadlines, applied to tax.

First, at the start of the year, put all four dates on the financial calendar with early reminders. Next, well before each date, confirm with the accountant that the amount and paperwork are ready. Finally, keep a record of each payment confirmation.

Take a second with this one. The accountant sends the quarterly amount the day before the deadline. It's much higher than last quarter, and Elias is unreachable. What do you do, and what do you change for next quarter?

frames.title: W-9/1099 Audits & Filing Deadlines
frames.text:
Get the vendor's tax form before you pay them the first time, not at tax time.

When a business pays contractors above a certain amount, it has to file year-end tax forms for them, using the details collected on a form called a W-9. Chasing a vendor for that in January is stressful and avoidable.

First, check the vendor list against the W-9 files now and then, especially for vendors added mid-year. Finally, put the year-end filing deadline on the calendar with plenty of lead time.

Now a scenario. In December, you find four contractors paid over the threshold with no W-9 on file. Two of them are hard to reach. What's your plan, week by week, to January?

frames.title: Financial Record Retention Requirements
frames.text:
Keeping records isn't enough; you have to be able to find them when someone asks.

Financial records have minimum periods they must be kept, and those vary by type and by state. Trust account records often have longer requirements. And destroying something too early can cause real trouble in an audit or dispute.

frames.title: Financial Record Retention Requirements
frames.text:
First, know the retention period for each type of record, not one rule for everything. Next, store records somewhere durable and searchable. Finally, build the retention date into the filing, so reviews happen on schedule.

Picture this. A partner wants to clear out the old storage room: 'Anything more than five years old can go.' The boxes include trust records and closed litigation files. What do you check before a single box leaves?

frames.title: Fraud Red Flags in Financial Documents
frames.text:
Most fraud doesn't look dramatic; it looks like a small, believable detail that's slightly off.

One odd detail is usually just a mistake. A pattern of odd details signals real trouble. And you see the most detail day to day, so you're often the first line of defense.

First, watch for the classic signs: an unfamiliar vendor, suspiciously round amounts, duplicate invoice numbers or sudden new bank details. Next, confirm any change in payment details through a separate channel you already trust, never the contact details in the request itself. Finally, raise a real concern promptly, rather than trying to solve it alone.

Here's one to think through. Last month, you flagged an invoice that turned out to be genuine, and you felt embarrassed. This month, an email from 'Elias' asks you to buy $1,500 in gift cards for a client, quickly and quietly. What do you do?

frames.title: Practice Lab
frames.text: Time to practice what you just learned. In today's lab, you'll reconcile a client trust ledger, audit a queue of invoices and bills, decide the right follow-up for every open invoice, then find the planted errors in a set of billing documents. It's your turn now.
